items.title: How Do I: Access NetScaler VPX and Console images in public cloud?
items.summary: Citrix is updating how customers access NetScaler VPX and NetScaler Console/Console-Agent images in public clouds. Access to selected cloud marketplace listings is moving from unrestricted public availability to a controlled access model.  If you deploy NetScaler from a public cloud marketplace, or your automation references marketplace images, this change may affect you. This guide explains the available access methods, how to request marketplace access, and what changes may be required for existing deployments and automation.  Note: This blog will update as the access process evolves, including Console image availability and other incremental updates.  What is changing? NetScaler VPX and Console/Console-Agent VM images are transitioning to controlled access on supported cloud marketplaces. Customers can obtain images through either of the following methods:  Citrix Downloads: Download the applicable image directly.  Cloud marketplaces: Access AWS limited offers or Azure private plans after Citrix verifies entitlement and enables access for the relevant cloud account.  The available method depends on the cloud provider and deployment scenario.  How do I access NetScaler images? Option 1: Download from Citrix Downloads Customers can directly download applicable NetScaler public cloud images from Citrix Downloads.  Note: NetScaler Console images are not yet listed on Citrix Downloads. Availability is planned separately.  AWS  AWS-compatible NetScaler images are not yet available on Citrix Downloads and will be added soon. In the meantime, AWS customers can request access to the AWS Marketplace limited offers described in Option 2.  Azure Citrix Downloads is the recommended access path for Azure Cloud Solution Provider (CSP) customers, as Azure CSP subscriptions do not support Marketplace private plans.  For more information, see Azure Marketplace private plans.  GCP Citrix Downloads is the only supported path for obtaining NetScaler images for GCP deployments.  Option 2: Access images through cloud marketplaces To deploy through AWS or Azure Marketplace, request access so Citrix can verify your entitlement and allowlist your cloud account. GCP Marketplace is not supported.  To request access, contact your Citrix representative or email netscaler-cloud-marketplace@citrix.com  and include your Citrix account ID and the relevant cloud account details:  AWS: AWS account ID  Azure: Subscription ID or tenant ID  AWS NetScaler VPX, NetScaler Agent, and NetScaler Console images are now available as Limited offers on AWS Marketplace.  Once access is enabled, use the applicable offer below.  New AWS Limited Offers  AWS Marketplace URL  NetScaler VPX (Customer Licensed)  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-xgdh6n3hztqze  NetScaler VPX 15.1 Tech Preview  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-on4be36na2hoi  NetScaler VPX FIPS ENA (Customer Licensed)  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-dja64jkutq2ru  NetScaler Agent (On-Prem)  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-mfvbswna3plko  NetScaler Agent (Service)  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-ac3vud4abobxc  NetScaler Console (Private Offer)  https://aws.amazon.com/marketplace/pp/prodview-5zzx3qxmjwswi  Azure NetScaler VPX images are now available as private plans on Azure Marketplace.   Once access is enabled, use the applicable private plan ID below.  Azure offer  Private plan ID  NetScaler VPX 14.1 BYOL  netscaler_141_byol_private  NetScaler VPX 13.1 BYOL  netscaler_131_byol_private  NetScaler VPX 14.1 FIPS BYOL  netscaler_141_fips_byol_private  NetScaler VPX 13.1 FIPS BYOL  netscaler_131_fips_byol_private  Note: Migration of NetScaler Console/Console-Agent VM images to Azure private plans is planned separately.   GCP GCP Marketplace does not natively support access-controlled VM listings this model requires. Consequently, NetScaler VPX images have already been deprecated on GCP Marketplace.  Use Citrix Downloads to obtain NetScaler images for GCP deployments.  Note: Deprecation of NetScaler Console/Console-Agent VM images is planned separately.  Frequently asked questions Why can't I access my VPX image even after my cloud account or subscription is allowlisted? You may still be referencing an outdated marketplace listing or plan ID. Ensure you are accessing the updated AWS limited offer or Azure private plan listed in this guide.  Why can't I deploy a Marketplace image after my cloud account or subscription is allowlisted? Your organization's cloud administrator may need to approve the new marketplace listing or private plan before it can be deployed. Since the marketplace offers and plans have changed, contact your cloud administrator to confirm that the updated listing or plan is approved for use.  Is Citrix creating a separate private offer for each customer? No. The access change uses access-controlled marketplace listings rather than creating a unique private offer for every customer.   What changes are required in my automation scripts after whitelisting? Changes should generally be minimal. Update your scripts to reference the applicable AWS limited listing ID or Azure private plan ID for the scripts to work. Citrix-provided Terraform scripts and cloud templates are a separate case. See the next question.  Will Terraform scripts and cloud templates for public cloud provisioning work? Not yet. Recent access changes affect Citrix-provided Terraform scripts and cloud templates for public cloud provisioning. We are updating them and will refresh this blog as soon as they are available.  I do not see latest CPX images on Quay. Are there any access restrictions for NetScaler CPX? Yes, NetScaler CPX images will no longer be publicly available on Quay. The latest images are available on Citrix Downloads and will soon be available through a private container registry.

items.title: Raising the security bar for public sector Citrix DaaS environments with Citrix deviceTRUST
items.summary: Why security in public sector DaaS requires a new approachPublic sector organizations face a unique combination of security challenges. They must protect highly sensitive data, comply with strict regulatory frameworks, and defend against increasingly sophisticated cyber threats—while still enabling modern workstyles such as remote access, third-party collaboration, and hybrid operations. Citrix DaaS Local (formerly CVAD) is a critical foundation for this strategy. By centralizing applications and data, it reduces endpoint exposure and helps enforce consistent security controls. However, as access scenarios become more dynamic, security requirements extend beyond simply granting or denying access at logon. Modern public sector security strategies - especially those aligned with Zero Trust - require continuous verification, adaptive enforcement, and the ability to respond to risk changes in real time. Citrix deviceTRUST extends the security model of Citrix DaaS by introducing real-time, context-aware access controls within the active session. Understanding the security gap in traditional VDI access modelsVDI architectures have historically focused on securing session establishment. Identity validation, MFA, and network controls ensure users are authenticated before access is granted. Once the session is active, conditions are typically assumed to remain stable. In today’s threat landscape, this assumption no longer holds true. Endpoint posture, network trust level, and user location can change during an active session. For example, a device may switch from a trusted network to unsecured Wi‑Fi, or critical security controls may be disabled. Traditional access models are not designed to evaluate or respond to these changes in real time. Security enforcement remains static while risk evolves dynamically. For public sector organizations supporting: ·         Remote and hybrid work ·         Contractors and partner access ·         Managed and unmanaged devices This gap becomes increasingly relevant. Closing it requires extending security enforcement into the active session—where risk actually occurs. Public sector security requirements in a Zero Trust worldPublic sector strategies increasingly align with Zero Trust principles: ·         Never assume trust ·         Continuously validate access ·         Enforce least privilege In practice, access decisions must go beyond identity and include device posture, network context, location, and time. These factors must be evaluated continuously—not just at authentication. Key requirements include: ·         Validate device compliance beyond logon ·         Restrict access based on network and geographic context ·         React immediately to changing risk conditions ·         Maintain auditability and consistent policy enforcement These requirements directly apply to VDI environments, where sessions are often long-running and interact with sensitive systems. Extending security inside the Citrix DaaS session with Citrix deviceTRUSTdeviceTRUST enhances Citrix DaaS by introducing real-time, contextual access controls within the session itself. Instead of relying solely on pre-authentication checks, it continuously evaluates signals such as: ·         Device security posture (e.g., firewall, antivirus, patch level) ·         Network context (e.g., trusted vs. untrusted connections) ·         Location and time-based conditions These signals are enforced through Citrix policies and session-level controls, allowing access to adapt dynamically as conditions change. This approach integrates natively with Citrix DaaS, leveraging standard HDX communication and requiring no architectural changes, making it well suited for regulated public sector environments. Public sector use cases: from static access to continuous protectionThe benefits of real-time, contextual access are best illustrated through practical use cases: Protecting access from insecure devices  If a device falls out of compliance (e.g., antivirus disabled), access can be immediately restricted within the active session. Network-aware access control  Security policies can adapt based on whether users connect via trusted networks or public Wi‑Fi. Geographic and jurisdictional controls  Access to sensitive systems can be restricted based on region or country, supporting data sovereignty requirements. Granular application protection  Instead of blocking entire sessions, access can be limited to specific applications based on risk conditions. These use cases focus on reducing risk without disrupting end-user productivity. Operational benefits for public sector IT teamsIn addition to enhanced security, Citrix deviceTRUST delivers practical operational benefits: ·         No additional infrastructure or SaaS dependency ·         Support for both managed and unmanaged devices ·         Immediate response to risk without manual intervention These capabilities are particularly valuable for public sector organizations with limited resources and strict change management processes. Getting started: low-risk, incremental adoptionCitrix deviceTRUST supports a phased approach to adoption. Organizations can begin with a focused set of high-impact use cases—such as blocking non-compliant devices—and expand over time. There is no need to redesign the Citrix DaaS architecture or disrupt existing workflows. Policies can be introduced incrementally and refined based on operational experience. Raising the security bar for public sector VDICitrix DaaS remains a core component of secure digital workspaces in the public sector. As threats evolve and Zero Trust strategies mature, security must move beyond static decisions toward continuous, context-aware enforcement. Citrix deviceTRUST enables organizations to align access with real-time risk, improving protection while maintaining usability—without adding complexity. Next stepsTo explore how this approach fits into your environment: ·         Review your current Citrix DaaS security model and identify gaps in session-level enforcement ·         Define 1–2 high-impact use cases (e.g., unmanaged devices or public network access) ·         Engage with your Citrix team to validate integration with your existing architecture ·         Plan a focused proof of concept to evaluate real-time policy enforcement in action Learn more at:  https://www.citrix.com/platform/devicetrust.html

items.title: How do I: Perform zero-downtime NetScaler upgrades using ISSU?
items.summary: A practical runbook for upgrading a NetScaler high-availability pair while preserving established connections Upgrading a NetScaler HA pair usually comes down to one risky moment: the failover between two nodes running different builds, when established connections can be dropped. ISSU is built to take that risk off the table. This article walks through the In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU) workflow for a two-node NetScaler high-availability (HA) deployment, covering the operational sequence, safeguards, validation points, and recovery decisions you need to minimize service interruption.    What are we talking about? In-Service Software Upgrade (ISSU) lets you upgrade a NetScaler HA pair without dropping established connections. During a standard HA upgrade there is a point where the two nodes run different builds, and mixed-build HA nodes cannot fail over existing connections normally. ISSU closes that gap by combining the role change with connection migration, which reduces the downtime risk. It is most valuable when established sessions must survive the HA role transition: payment and banking transactions, critical application sessions, VPN or ICA sessions, WebSocket connections, database connections, streaming flows, and other long-lived sessions whose interruption could cause a failed transaction, user disruption, or costly recovery.  ISSU introduces a migration phase. The upgraded secondary becomes the new primary and receives requests and responses for existing connections, but steers those flows through a GRE tunnel to the old primary. If an HA SYNC VLAN is configured, the migration traffic uses that VLAN; a dedicated HA SYNC VLAN is optional. The old primary continues processing those established connections and sends traffic toward the destination, while new connections are handled by the upgraded primary. Migration completes after the old connections close, allowing the old primary, now secondary, to be upgraded.   Figure 1. During ISSU migration, the upgraded primary handles new connections while established connections continue on the old primary through the GRE/SYNC VLAN path until they close.   Eligibility and pre-upgrade planning Prerequisites Before you schedule the change, make sure you have: a healthy two-node NetScaler HA pair; a functioning traffic path between the nodes, either an HA SYNC VLAN or the GRE tunnel used for migration; a supported direct upgrade path from your source build to the target build for your appliance platform and licensed features; console access to both nodes; and current backups stored off the appliance.   Validate the procedure and exact commands against the documentation for the target release and build. The checklist below covers each readiness check in detail.  Pre-upgrade readiness checklist  Area  Required check  Topology  Confirm a healthy two-node HA pair; identify the current primary and secondary; confirm all intended interfaces and HA monitors are up.  Compatibility  Confirm the target release/build supports the appliance model, VPX hypervisor or MPX hardware, enabled features, and the intended direct upgrade path.  Build behavior  Review release notes and the internal HA-version change information for the source and target builds. Plan for HA synchronization functions to be restricted while builds differ.  Licensing  Verify that licensing remains valid on the target build and that any required licensing-framework migration is complete before the change.  Capacity  Verify that either node can safely carry new traffic during the migration and that the old primary can continue processing established connections until they drain.  Disk and hardware  Resolve disk errors and ensure sufficient free space. NetScaler Console guidance calls for at least 6 GB free in /var and 200 MB in /flash for its upgrade workflow.  Configuration  Run a final HA synchronization while both nodes are on the same build, save the configuration, and verify that startup configuration and running configuration agree.  Customizations  Inventory and back up customized files, especially under /etc. Follow the documented procedure for preserving and reapplying customizations.  Backups  Create full and basic backups, copy them off the appliance, preserve the current firmware image, and document console access and rollback decision points.  Observability  Record a baseline for virtual-server state, service state, connection counts, throughput, CPU, memory, SSL errors, authentication success, and synthetic application checks.    Zero-downtime upgrade runbook Command conventions. Run NetScaler commands at the appliance CLI prompt. Commands prefixed with # run in the FreeBSD shell after entering shell. Replace values in angle brackets with the approved build, file, interface, or object name. Confirm syntax with man <command> on the target build before execution.  Step 1 — Prepare and freeze the environment Confirm the change window, owners, monitoring coverage, application test path, and escalation contacts.  Stop nonessential configuration changes. Save the NetScaler configuration and confirm the HA pair is healthy and synchronized.  Identify the current primary and secondary nodes. Do not proceed if either node is in STAYPRIMARY or STAYSECONDARY unless the documented design specifically requires it and the state has been reviewed.  Capture backups and baseline evidence. Copy backup packages off the appliances.  Stage the approved target build and verify integrity, free space, compatibility, and release-note prerequisites.  show ns version  show ha node  show interface  show channel  show ns ip  show route  show lb vserver  show serviceGroup  show ns config  save ns config  create system backup pre_issu_<date> -level full  sync ha files all  shell  # df -h /var /flash  # ls -lh /var/nsinstall  # exit  Step 2 — Upgrade the current secondary (Can be done with Upgrade Jobs easily) NetScaler Console option. Create or schedule an Upgrade NetScaler instances maintenance job for the current secondary. Review and clear the Console pre-validation results before starting the job. For an HA pair, upgrade the nodes in separate stages so the remaining node is upgraded only after ISSU migration and connection draining are complete.    Upgrade the current secondary. Connect directly to the NSIP of the node that show ha node identifies as SECONDARY. Install the target build on this node first, using either your standard firmware installation procedure or the NetScaler Console upgrade job described above. Do not begin with the current primary.  Allow the node to reboot fully. Verify management access, expected software version, interface and channel state, routing, services, virtual servers, licenses, certificates, and system health.  Confirm that the upgraded node is secondary and that the existing primary continues serving production traffic. Do not make configuration changes while the nodes run different builds unless the change plan explicitly accounts for disabled synchronization and propagation.  If any critical check fails, stop. Restore the secondary to the approved pre-change state before attempting migration.  show ns version  show ha node  show interface  show lb vserver  show serviceGroup  Step 3 — Initiate ISSU migration From the upgraded secondary, start the ISSU migration by running start ns migration, as shown in the commands below, or by using the equivalent control in the GUI of the target build. Confirm the exact syntax against the product documentation for that build.  Verify that roles change as expected: the upgraded node becomes primary and the old primary becomes secondary.  Confirm that new connections are accepted and processed by the upgraded primary. Verify that established connections continue through the migration path to the old primary.  Monitor both nodes continuously: HA state, migration state, established connection counts, GRE or SYNC VLAN reachability, packet drops, resets, application response, authentication, SSL handshakes, CPU, and memory.  Do not upgrade or reboot the old primary while migrated connections remain. Long-lived sessions may extend this phase; use a pre-agreed maximum drain time and application-specific decision criteria.  start ns migration  show ns migration  show ha node  Step 4 — Complete connection draining Migration is complete when the established connections that existed before the role change have closed and the old primary is no longer required to process them. Confirm this with appliance state and application monitoring; do not rely on elapsed time alone. If the environment contains long-lived ICA, VPN, WebSocket, database, or streaming sessions, coordinate acceptable drain behavior with application owners before the change.  show ns migration  show ns migration -dumpsession YES  stat system  stat cpu  stat lb vserver  stat serviceGroup  Step 5 — Upgrade the remaining node NetScaler Console option. After migrated sessions have drained, create or run the second upgrade job for the former primary, now secondary. Use the same approved target build, review the pre-validation results, and do not run this job concurrently with the first-node upgrade.  Upgrade the former primary second. After ISSU migration has completed and migrated sessions have drained, connect directly to the NSIP of the old primary, which is now SECONDARY. Run the same firmware installation sequence and install the identical target release and build used on the first node.  After reboot, verify that both nodes report the identical software build, normal HA status, and expected interface, routing, licensing, service, and virtual-server state.  Restore or reapply approved customizations using the documented post-upgrade procedure.  Re-enable normal operational activity only after synchronization, command propagation, state exchange, connection mirroring, and persistence synchronization have returned to their expected state.  show ns version  show ha node  show interface  show channel  show lb vserver  show serviceGroup  show ns migration  sync ha files all  save ns config   Post-upgrade validation Post-upgrade acceptance criteria  Layer  Acceptance test  HA  Both nodes are UP, roles are correct, builds match, and synchronization has completed without unresolved errors.  Network  Interfaces, channels, VLANs, routes, ARP/ND state, and upstream/downstream reachability match the approved baseline.  Applications  Critical virtual servers and services are UP; synthetic transactions succeed; persistence, redirects, content switching, and responder/rewrite behavior are correct.  Security  TLS negotiation, certificate chains, authentication flows, gateway access, WAF policy behavior, and security logging are healthy.  Operations  Monitoring, SNMP, syslog, analytics, backups, administrative access, and NetScaler Console visibility operate normally.  Stability  No unexplained rise in resets, errors, latency, CPU, memory, packet drops, or support events during the defined observation period.    Rollback and troubleshooting Before migration: If the upgraded secondary fails validation, keep production on the original primary. Diagnose the failure or return the secondary to the approved source build and restore its configuration before retrying.  After migration: Avoid an improvised failback while connections are being steered between mixed-version nodes. Use the documented recovery path for the exact release/build, and involve NetScaler Support if established connections, HA state, or configuration integrity is at risk. The safest action may be to stabilize traffic on the upgraded primary, allow existing sessions to drain, and then decide whether to complete or reverse the change.  Exceptional controls: These commands can interrupt or discard migrated sessions. Use them only under a documented rollback or recovery decision and after checking the command reference for the running build.  stop ns migration  complete ns migration  Warning: complete ns migration force-completes the operation and cleans up active migrated connections; it is not the normal drain-completion step.  For an upgrade incident, preserve configuration files from both appliances, relevant newnslog files, ns.log, the system messages file, the exact source and target builds, timestamps, console output, and a network topology diagram. Common failure areas include unsupported MPX or VPX combinations, hardware or file-system errors, insufficient space in /var, and configuration or customization mismatches.   Important limitations and operating practices ISSU applies to supported HA upgrade scenarios; it is not a general method for upgrading a standalone appliance or every deployment topology.  A healthy HA control plane and a functioning traffic path between nodes are prerequisites. A broken SYNC VLAN or migration tunnel can compromise connection preservation.  While builds differ, do not assume normal HA synchronization behavior. Make no unplanned configuration changes during this interval.  ISSU preserves existing connections through migration; it cannot guarantee application success if the target build changes feature behavior, policy syntax, cipher support, or external dependencies.  Long-lived sessions can delay completion. Establish a business-approved drain policy instead of terminating sessions unexpectedly.  After both nodes are upgraded, run a controlled failover test only if it is included in the approved plan and application owners are ready to validate service.   Change record template Item  Value  Source build / target build    Primary / secondary NSIP    Backup location    Baseline completed    Secondary upgrade completed    ISSU migration started / completed    Old primary drained    Remaining node upgraded    Post-checks passed    Rollback owner and decision deadline      Official NetScaler documentation In Service Software Upgrade support for high availability for performing zero downtime upgrade  Upgrade a high availability pair  Use jobs to upgrade NetScaler instances in NetScaler Console  Troubleshooting installation, upgrade, and downgrade issues  Configuring high availability  NetScaler CLI command reference: ns-migration

items.title: Protecting Customers: Immediate Guidance for CVE-2026-107406 in NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway
items.summary: Today, Citrix published a critical security bulletin for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway regarding CVE-2026-107406.  CVE-2026-107406 is a memory overflow vulnerability that may lead to remote code execution or denial of service under specific configuration conditions. The issue carries a CVSS v4.0 base score of 9.5 and is rated Critical. We strongly urge affected customers to review the advisory and upgrade impacted NetScaler instances to the recommended versions as soon as possible. As of the publication of the bulletin, Citrix is not aware of any unmitigated exploits of this vulnerability.   What is affected The following supported versions of Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway are affected by the vulnerability if they meet the following conditions:   NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway must be configured as a SAML SP or SAML IdP, subject to the following version-specific requirements:  For the following versions: Applicable only when configured as a SAML IdP:  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway between 14.1-73.37 and 14.1-73.41, inclusive  NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS between 14.1-73.37 FIPS and 14.1-73.41 FIPS, inclusive  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway between 13.1-64.23 and 13.1-64.28, inclusive  NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS between 13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.279 and 13.1- 37.282, inclusive    For the following versions: Applicable only when configured as a SAML SP or SAML IdP:  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway before 14.1-73.37   NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS before 14.1-73.37 FIPS   NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway before 13.1-64.23  NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS before13.1-NDcPP 13.1-37.279     Secure Private Access Hybrid deployments using NetScaler instances are also affected and should be upgraded to the recommended NetScaler versions. The bulletin does not apply to Citrix-managed cloud services or Citrix-managed Adaptive Authentication, which Citrix upgrades with the necessary software updates.   When the vulnerability applies Customers can determine whether their NetScaler deployment is configured as a SAML identity provider (IdP) or service provider (SP) by checking its configuration for entries matching either of the following:  Appliance is configured as a SAML SP  add authentication samlAction  Appliance is configured as a SAML IdP  add authentication samlIdPProfile   What customers should do now Customers should prioritize upgrading affected NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments to the fixed builds listed in the security bulletin as applicable to their environment. The following flow chart can help you determine if you need to upgrade your NetScaler deployment:    *Please note that this flow chart is intended to help you follow the instructions in the security bulletin; the security bulletin remains the primary source for addressing the vulnerability. Where can I learn more about the vulnerabilities announced earlier and the affected NetScaler software versions? You can refer to the blogs published for CVE 2026-88779 and CVE 2026-88771 through CVE 2026-88778 and the corresponding security bulletins. items.title: Post-quantum cryptography architectural considerations
items.summary: Part 1: Pure vs. hybrid post-quantum cryptography First in a series on post-quantum cryptography architectural considerations for architects and engineers designing encryption for the pre-quantum era while preparing for post-quantum protection.  Why this matters now Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) is no longer a theoretical architecture topic. NIST has finalized the first PQC standards for key establishment and digital signatures, including ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA. Government guidance from CISA, NSA, and NIST also emphasizes that organizations should begin preparing now because migration will take time and adversaries may already be collecting encrypted traffic for future decryption.  This is the harvest now, decrypt later phase: encrypted data captured today may become readable later if quantum-vulnerable public-key cryptography protects it and the data must remain confidential long enough for a cryptographically relevant quantum computer to emerge. For architects and engineers, the practical question is no longer whether to plan for PQC, but how to transition without breaking existing systems, protocols, devices, clients, or operational processes.  The architectural choice: Pure PQC, hybrid PQC, or hybrid-to-pure At a high level, organizations have three architectural patterns to consider: pure PQC, hybrid PQC, and a phased roadmap that starts with hybrid PQC and ends with pure PQC. Pure PQC is the long-term destination because it removes dependence on classical public-key algorithms that are vulnerable to quantum attacks. Hybrid PQC is often the more feasible near-term path because it combines post-quantum algorithms with established classical algorithms, which preserves compatibility while adding quantum-resistant protection.  This distinction matters because real enterprise and government environments contain long-lived technology stacks: older operating systems, embedded devices, legacy clients, constrained appliances, custom applications, regulated workloads, and vendor dependencies that cannot all adopt post-quantum algorithms at the same pace. Post-quantum keys, ciphertexts, and signatures can also be significantly larger than their classical equivalents, which can affect handshake size, protocol limits, latency, memory usage, certificate chains, packet fragmentation, and operational telemetry.  Comparison chart Architecture  Pros  Cons  Best fit  Pure PQC  Strongest long-term alignment with post-quantum standards; removes dependence on quantum-vulnerable RSA, DH, ECDH, and ECDSA for covered use cases; simplifies future-state security posture once the ecosystem is ready.  May not interoperate with older clients, operating systems, appliances, libraries, certificates, and protocols; larger keys and signatures can affect performance and packet sizing; vendor and compliance readiness may vary.  Modern, controlled environments where endpoints, libraries, protocols, certificates, and operational tooling can all support post-quantum algorithms.  Hybrid PQC  Adds post-quantum protection while retaining classical algorithm compatibility; reduces migration risk; enables early defense against harvest now, decrypt later; provides a practical bridge for mixed environments.  More complex to implement, test, monitor, and explain; may increase handshake size and operational overhead; still carries classical cryptography as part of the construction until the environment is ready to remove it.  Enterprises and government agencies with mixed endpoint populations, legacy dependencies, phased procurement cycles, or strict availability requirements.  Hybrid-to-pure roadmap  Balances near-term risk reduction with long-term architectural clarity; allows inventory, testing, vendor engagement, policy updates, and phased deprecation of classical algorithms; supports measurable milestones.  Requires governance, cryptographic inventory, dependency tracking, exception management, and clear retirement criteria; can become permanent if the organization does not define an end state.  Most large organizations that need to start protecting sensitive traffic now while planning an orderly migration to pure PQC over time.  Decision tree for architects  Start  Decision  Yes →  No →  Architecture direction  1  Does the data need to remain confidential for years or decades?  Prioritize PQC now because the workload may be exposed to harvest now, decrypt later risk.  Continue discovery and prioritize based on sensitivity, exposure, and business criticality.  Move to PQC planning immediately for long-lived sensitive data.  2  Can all endpoints, clients, operating systems, libraries, and appliances support PQC today?  Evaluate pure PQC for controlled production use.  Start with hybrid PQC and document blockers to pure PQC.  Pure PQC if the ecosystem is ready; hybrid PQC if compatibility is required.  3  Are legacy systems, embedded clients, constrained devices, or third-party dependencies in the path?  Use hybrid PQC as the transition architecture and track each dependency.  Continue validating pure PQC readiness.  Hybrid PQC is the safer bridge for mixed environments.  4  Can the protocol and infrastructure tolerate larger keys, ciphertexts, signatures, and handshakes?  Proceed to pilot rollout with monitoring.  Benchmark, tune, and update protocol, network, or certificate assumptions before scaling.  Pilot before broad deployment.  5  Is the workload regulated or tied to government requirements?  Align algorithm choices, evidence collection, validation status, and timelines with applicable policy.  Use internal risk appetite and data sensitivity to set migration priority.  Map the architecture to compliance and audit expectations.  6  Can operations monitor, troubleshoot, and support the new cryptographic posture?  Expand rollout by workload and user group.  Update telemetry, logging, runbooks, incident response, and support workflows before production rollout.  Operational readiness is required before scale.  7  Is there a defined retirement point for classical fallback?  Use a hybrid-to-pure roadmap with milestones and exit criteria.  Create governance so Hybrid remains a bridge, not the destination.  Target state: pure PQC.  A practical roadmap from hybrid to pure A pragmatic roadmap starts with cryptographic discovery: identify where public-key cryptography is used for TLS, VPN, SSH, code signing, certificates, key exchange, device trust, authentication, and long-lived data protection. Next, prioritize systems based on data sensitivity, confidentiality lifetime, exposure, user population, and operational criticality. Systems protecting long-lived sensitive information should move first.  From there, organizations can introduce hybrid PQC in controlled environments, validate interoperability, monitor performance, and expand deployment by workload. During this phase, architecture teams should define the target pure PQC state, document exceptions, track vendor readiness, and set criteria for retiring classical fallback. The transition succeeds only when hybrid PQC becomes a bridge, not a destination.  Citrix perspective: Start protecting now The Citrix DaaS platform supports both pure PQC and hybrid PQC options, giving customers architectural flexibility based on their readiness, risk posture, and endpoint environment. This matters because organizations should not have to choose between waiting for every legacy dependency to modernize and taking meaningful action against harvest now, decrypt later risk today.  Citrix is uniquely positioned among Desktop as a Service (DaaS) providers to support pure PQC for Windows 11 because its cryptographic module implementation is based on OpenSSL rather than Schannel. That architectural choice gives customers a path to adopt post-quantum encryption sooner, including scenarios where pure PQC is appropriate and where hybrid PQC is the safer transition architecture.  The most important takeaway is simple: Customers do not have to wait for the post-quantum era to begin protecting themselves. The harvest now, decrypt later threat is already relevant for sensitive, long-lived data. A well-designed hybrid-to-pure roadmap lets organizations reduce risk now, maintain compatibility during the transition, and move toward a pure PQC future as the ecosystem matures.

items.title: Citrix Experience Insights Flex: Managed Observability for the Modern Workspace
items.summary: Every day, Citrix administrators and EUC teams deal with the same types of questions: Why is this user slow? Is the issue on the endpoint, the network, the application, or the Citrix session? Did performance change after an update? Is the problem affecting one user or hundreds?  Citrix Experience Insights Flex brings performance, user experience, and security telemetry together in a Citrix managed analytics platform powered by Splunk Cloud. With predefined dashboards and deep visibility across sessions, endpoints, applications, networks, browsers, users, processes, and network connections, teams can move faster from a symptom or suspicious behavior to the underlying cause.  This makes Experience Insights useful not only for troubleshooting and root cause analysis, but also for validating changes, understanding application behavior, and supporting security investigations.  The telemetry can be collected from virtual and physical environments, including Citrix DaaS, Azure Virtual Desktop, Windows 365, desktops, and laptops.   What can you observe? Experience Insights provides detailed visibility across three key areas:  User experience: Session performance, logons, boot times, and overall experience.  Endpoint and applications: CPU, memory, disk, application performance, responsiveness, hangs, crashes, and process behavior.  Network and security context: Network quality, browser and SaaS performance, user activity, process relationships, network connections, and other endpoint signals.  This deeper telemetry is especially valuable when troubleshooting issues across multiple layers or validating changes such as Windows image updates, application rollouts, AVD or Windows 365 migrations, and security deployments.  Teams can compare performance before and after a change, identify what is improved or degraded, and understand the impact on the user experience.  This is where observability goes beyond troubleshooting and becomes a tool for continuous improvement and change validation.   A managed observability model One of the biggest advantages of Experience Insights Flex is its operating model.  Citrix manages the Splunk Cloud analytics backend, capacity, platform updates, and predefined dashboards.  The customer focuses on deploying the agent, controlling telemetry collection, managing access, and using the data.  This removes several common blockers in observability projects:  Analytics platform procurement  Backend administration  Dashboard development  Scaling and capacity planning  Access dependency on another IT team  The result is a much faster path from deployment to useful insights.   Citrix Director and Experience Insights Flex: better together During customer engagements, I often get the question: “If we already have Director or Monitor, why do we need Experience Insights?”  The answer is simple: they complement each other.  Director/Monitor is where support teams typically start. It helps them identify and triage issues with Citrix sessions, machines, logons, and infrastructure.   Experience Insights Flex takes the investigation deeper by adding endpoint, application, browser, network, and workspace telemetry.  For example, when a user reports a slow Citrix DaaS session, the Help Desk can identify the issue in Director/Monitor. If deeper analysis is needed, IT or engineering teams can use Experience Insights Flex to determine whether the root cause is the endpoint, network, application, or another dependency.   Takeaways Citrix Experience Insights Flex brings together:  High resolution workspace telemetry  Citrix-managed Splunk Cloud analytics  Predefined dashboards  Endpoint, application, network, browser, security and session visibility  Different levels of data analysis:  For EUC administrators, it extends troubleshooting beyond the session.  For engineers and architects, it provides deeper root cause analysis and historical context.  For IT leadership, it delivers workspace observability without the operational burden of building and managing another analytics platform.  Spend less time managing the observability platform and more time understanding and improving the user /persona experience. items.title: Understanding and Addressing CVE-2026-88779 in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway
items.summary: CVE-2026-88779 is a memory overflow vulnerability in Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway that can lead to denial of service under specific deployment conditions. The issue affects customer-managed NetScaler deployments running affected supported versions when the required preconditions are met. Customers should review their deployed versions and configurations, then install the relevant updated versions as soon as possible.  Affected Versions The following supported versions are affected when the CVE preconditions (see the section “How to Determine Whether a NetScaler deployment Meets the Preconditions” below) apply:  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 14.1 before 14.1-73.41  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 13.1 before 13.1-64.28  NetScaler ADC FIPS before 14.1-73.41 FIPS  NetScaler ADC FIPS and NDcPP before 13.1-37.282  What Is the Issue? CVE-2026-88779 is categorized as CWE-119: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer. The vulnerability has a CVSS v4.0 base score of 8.7. Citrix has observed targeted attacks on unmitigated NetScaler deployments which can lead to Denial of Service.  If the condition is triggered repeatedly, the service may remain unavailable. Our analysis indicates that this issue affects service availability, and we have not identified an impact on the integrity of customer data. Citrix strongly urges all customers to install the latest versions as soon as possible.  The most important operational detail is that exposure depends on how the NetScaler deployment is configured. Customers should validate whether the relevant Gateway, AAA, and SAML preconditions apply to their environment.  Please note that the bulletin only applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. Citrix upgrades the Citrix-managed cloud services, including Gateway Service and Citrix-managed Adaptive Authentication, with the necessary software updates.  How to Determine Whether a NetScaler Deployment Meets the Preconditions The issue is associated with NetScaler deployments that use SAML authentication in conjunction with Gateway or AAA functionality. Customers who have deployed NetScaler as a Gateway or AAA virtual server should review their NetScaler configurations to determine whether SAML authentication actions are configured.  Customers can determine whether their NetScaler deployment meets the precondition by inspecting their NetScaler configuration for entries matching either of the following:  Appliance is configured as a SAML SP   add authentication samlAction    			OR    Appliance is configured as a SAML IdP   add authentication samlIdPProfile  What Customers Should Do  As a mitigation, Citrix has released signatures which can be used via the Global Deny List feature. This can help reduce exposure while customers validate applicability and plan an upgrade to a software version containing the fix.   The Global Deny List feature is enabled by default on NetScaler software starting with versions 14.1-60.52 and 13.1-63.21. Here are the prerequisites:  You need to use NetScaler Console on-premises (with Cloud Connect) or NetScaler Console service.  Please ensure that the “Virtual patching” Status is “Enabled” in the NetScaler Console configurable settings as shown below:  Applicable NetScaler software versions must fall within one of the following supported version ranges:  14.1 version range: >= 14.1-73.37 and < 14.1-73.41  13.1 version range: >= 13.1-64.23 and < 13.1-64.28   Verify if Global Deny List signatures are available on your NetScaler deployment by executing the following command:  show appfw signatures   In the output, verify under “Name: *Default Signatures” that the Encrypted Version is displayed as a number. This signifies that a version of the signatures is available on a NetScaler deployment. The version number needs to be at least v24 as shown below:   To verify whether the Global Deny List signature is working, please execute the following command in the NetScaler CLI:   stat denylist global AAA_REQUEST   Also check the counters statistics for the rule evaluated and other stats, including Last Hit Time. If the value is greater than 0, the rules are working.   IMPORTANT: Please also note that the Global Deny List signatures can help to mitigate the vulnerability. Citrix recommends upgrading to the following software versions containing the fix as soon as possible.  Upgrade NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 14.1 to 14.1-73.41 or later.  Upgrade NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 13.1 to 13.1-64.28 or later.  Upgrade NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS to 14.1-73.41 FIPS or later.  Upgrade NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP to 13.1-37.282 or later.  Additional Guidance Citrix continues to monitor vulnerability activity and to work with the security research community through coordinated disclosure. Citrix will continue to provide timely updates as needed to help customers protect their NetScaler deployments.   Customers should ensure that NetScaler deployments are updated promptly, review configurations against the applicable preconditions, and follow their standard incident response processes if they identify signs of compromise.  Customers can block suspicious IP addresses by using the blocklist functionality of NetScaler.  As part of a defense-in-depth approach, customers should review relevant network and perimeter controls and, where appropriate, use firewall rules to block traffic from IP addresses identified as sources of attack activity.  If you upgraded your NetScaler deployment with one of the updated software releases identified in the security bulletin for CVE 2026-88771 through CVE 2026-88778, and if you have determined that your NetScaler deployment meets the preconditions describe above, please upgrade your deployment again with the software released as part of the security bulletin for CVE-2026-88779 .  The official security bulletin for CVE 2026-88779 is the authoritative statement concerning the security vulnerability announced in the bulletin; please refer to the bulletin as the controlling statement concerning the vulnerability.  Learn more and stay up to date  Review the official security bulletin  Sign up for security bulletin notifications  Review the NetScaler Secure Deployment Guide  Use NetScaler Console security advisory for your NetScaler deployments.
