items.title: Understanding NetScaler Indicators of Compromise: What the IoC Feature Does, How It Evolves, and How to Interpret Results
items.summary: When a security bulletin is published, customers usually want to know three things quickly:   A clear mitigation path   A way to assess whether their environment shows signs of known compromise   Practical guidance on what to do next.   Concurrently with the publication of the recent NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway security bulletin, Citrix made Indicators of Compromise (IoC) scanning available through NetScaler Console and through support to help customers perform an initial assessment concerning the vulnerabilities identified in the bulletin across their NetScaler deployments.  This blog explains the IoC feature in NetScaler, how its detection logic evolves, why scan results may vary across versions, and how to interpret potential false positives.  What the IoC feature is designed to do The IoC feature in NetScaler Console provides an automated way to scan NetScaler instances for indicators of compromise. It helps customers identify known artifacts or activity patterns that may warrant further investigation.  For Console-managed deployments, the IoC workflow is available from the Security Advisory experience in NetScaler Console. Customers can initiate the scan, review results, and export a report for further analysis. For environments that cannot use NetScaler Console or that are air-gapped, customers should open a support case.  It is important to understand what the IoC feature is and what it is not. The IoC scan is an initial detection aid. It is not a substitute for a complete forensic investigation, and the absence of IoCs in the results does not rule out the possibility that an appliance was compromised. Threat actors can change tactics, techniques, procedures, and artifacts over time, and no indicator set can cover all possible compromise scenarios. The IoC feature will not indicate whether that the threat vector has moved laterally into adjacent systems and cannot determine if that may happen in the future. If a compromise is suspected, customers should preserve relevant evidence and engage their incident response or forensic team.  Why IoC logic may change after initial release IoC detection logic is updated as additional information becomes available. This is expected during any active security response. Early detection logic may prioritize speed and coverage for the most relevant indicators known at the time of release. As field reports, support cases, engineering analysis, and additional threat intelligence become available, Citrix may refine the logic to improve accuracy, reduce false positives, add new checks, and improve platform handling.  Customers may therefore see a newer IoC version become available after an earlier scan. The Console experience displays the detection logic version or release date used for newly initiated scans. If a newer version is available, customers should run a new scan rather than relying only on prior results.   This does not mean earlier scan results were invalid. It means the detection content has evolved as part of the response process. Customers should use the latest available IoC logic for the most current assessment.  Customers who need additional context can download the detailed scan results in PDF or CSV format by selecting the CSV/PDF link for each instance. The detailed report is useful because the high-level Console summary is intentionally concise and may not provide enough information for security teams to understand what was evaluated, which indicators were matched, which appliance or platform was involved, or which IoC logic version was used. Customers may need these details to correlate scan findings with appliance logs, SIEM alerts, file integrity data, support bundles, change records, or incident response timelines. The exported results can also help security teams distinguish between confirmed findings, potential false positives, unsupported-platform behavior, stale artifacts, or evidence that requires deeper forensic review.   Understanding results: “No potential compromise detected” does not mean “never compromised” A clean IoC result means that the scan did not find the specific indicators covered by that version of the detection logic at the time the scan ran. That is a useful signal, but it should not be interpreted as proof that the appliance was never targeted, never exposed, or never compromised.  If a customer has other evidence of suspicious activity, such as unexpected file changes, anomalous logs, unexplained core dumps, suspicious web content, credential theft concerns, or alerts from a third-party security tool, the absence of IoC findings should not override that evidence. In those cases, customers should continue with their incident response process and follow guidance for suspected compromise. Moreover, in cases where NetScaler may have been compromised, it’s possible that a threat actor may have attempted to cover their tracks and possibly succeeded in that attempt. To reduce the risk of such a scenario, Citrix strongly recommends customers to enable external logging to a SIEM platform for NetScaler.  Similarly, applying a software update addresses the published vulnerabilities going forward, but it does not remove potential compromise artifacts or prove that exploitation did not occur before the update. If compromise is suspected or confirmed, Citrix recommends deploying a new, updated NetScaler instance rather than relying on the update as a cleanup or remediation mechanism. For more details, please refer to the following support article.   IOC Version change log A positive IoC result indicates that the scan found something matching the detection logic. Customers should treat this as a signal that requires investigation, not as a definitive declaration of compromise in all cases.  Based on continuous feedback from customers during active security response, Citrix has refined the IoC logic to reduce false positives and expand support for Linux- based VPXs deployed on Nutanix. Below is a change log of IoC script versions for reference:    Version  Release Date   Change Log Comments  v1  September 27, 2026  Initial IOC script release for FreeBSD-based NetScaler platforms.  v2  September 28, 2026  Added platform validation to prevent execution on unsupported Linux-based deployments.  v3  September 29, 2026  Added support for VPX-Linux on AHV (14.1), reduced false positives through refined detection logic, and introduced additional IOC signatures. Recommended for all new deployments.  v4  October 1, 2026  Reduced false positives through refined detection logic. IOC findings are now categorized by severity (HIGH, MEDIUM, LOW) to help prioritize investigation.  v5 October 6, 2026 Additional IoC’s added. Note: When executing v4 via NetScaler Console or via the shell script directly on NetScaler appliances, customers may see the following entry in the IoC results even when the final summary output displays, “No compromise detected”:  Detected - Suspicious nobody processes: Potentially Compromised message: MEDIUM indicator of compromise: Suspicious processes found. path: [-] nobody <defunct>  Platform support and version considerations The IoC capability has evolved across versions. Customers should be aware of the following practical considerations:  NetScaler Console service and supported Console on-premises deployments with Cloud Connect can receive updated IoC content through the Console workflow.  The Console itself does not require an upgrade before updated IoC content is available, provided it is connected to the cloud service.  Customers should upgrade NetScaler appliances to the fixed builds identified in the security bulletin. The IoC scan should not be treated as a replacement for applying the update.  Air-gapped customers or customers unable to use Console should open a support case for assistance.  What customers should do if the scan detects potential compromise If the IoC scan reports potential compromise, customers should engage their security or incident response team, as Citrix Support is not positioned to perform forensic interpretation of IoC output. We recommend that you follow the guidance of your security or incident response team, but the following are some helpful basic tips:  Preserve evidence before making destructive changes. Retain logs, support bundles, snapshots, and relevant security telemetry where possible.  Review the detailed scan report and correlate the finding with appliance logs, file integrity monitoring results, SIEM data, and any third-party security findings.  Do not assume that applying the update removes compromise artifacts.  If compromise is suspected or confirmed, deploy a new, updated NetScaler instance and migrate configuration using a controlled, security-reviewed process. Please follow this article to do this.  Rotate credentials, certificates, keys, and secrets as appropriate based on the Enterprise incident response procedures.  Continue monitoring for suspicious activity after the new instance is deployed.  Customers must not rely on HA synchronization from a suspected compromised appliance as a remediation method without careful review. If an appliance is suspected to be compromised, configuration migration should be handled deliberately and reviewed by the customer’s security team.  What customers should do if the scan does not detect compromise If the scan reports no potential compromise detected, customers should still ensure they have completed the required software update. The IoC scan is not a replacement for patching.  Customers should also consider the broader context of their environment. If there are no other signs of suspicious activity, a clean scan result can provide another useful datapoint. However, if the customer has independent evidence of suspicious activity, they should continue their incident response process even if the IoC scan is clean.  Why customers may see different results after re-running the scan Customers may see different results across scans for several reasons, which may include the following:  The IoC detection logic was updated between scan runs.  The appliance was upgraded, rebuilt, or failed over between scans.  Additional logs or files became available or rotated out.  The earlier scan was run on an unsupported or partially supported platform.  The latest version removed checks that were producing low-confidence or false-positive results.  The latest version added checks for newly identified indicators or platform-specific artifacts.  For these reasons, customers should record the time of each scan, the IoC version or date shown in Console, the appliance build, and the platform type when reviewing results with their security team.  Common customer questions Does the product update clean up known IoCs? No. The update addresses the published vulnerabilities, but it should not be considered a clean-up mechanism for an appliance that may already be compromised. Installing the update does not remove potential compromise artifacts and does not prove that exploitation did not occur before the update.  Can Citrix confirm whether my appliance is compromised? The IoC scan can identify known indicators, but it cannot conclusively prove or disprove compromise. Customers should rely on their incident response or forensic team for a full compromise assessment.  Why did my appliance show a potential IoC after I upgraded? In some cases, the scan may detect log entries or artifacts associated with attempted exploitation that occurred after the appliance was updated or that do not by themselves prove successful compromise. Citrix has refined detection logic to reduce false positives. Customers should re-run the scan using the latest IoC logic and review the result with their security team.  Why did a rebuilt or newly deployed VPX show an IoC result? A rebuilt instance may still show results depending on how it was built, what configuration or files were restored, what logs were present, what platform was used, and which IoC logic version was run. If results are unexpected, customers should verify the IoC version, confirm platform support, and review whether any configuration, backups, files, or logs were carried over from a potentially affected system.  Are all IoCs publicly listed? Citrix provides IoC detection capabilities and published guidance, but detailed detection logic or a full comparison of indicator changes between versions may not be published. Customers should use the latest Citrix-provided IoC workflow and combine it with their own security monitoring and incident response process.  Does a clean scan mean I do not need to upgrade? No. Customers should upgrade to the updated product builds identified in the security bulletin regardless of IoC scan outcome. The IoC scan is for assessment; the update is for addressing the vulnerabilities.  Our commitment to continued refinement Citrix continues to refine IoC detection as new information becomes available. That includes improving accuracy, reducing false positives, adding platform-specific handling where appropriate, and clarifying customer guidance. Security response is an iterative process, and IoC content may be updated as investigations progress and as customer environments provide additional evidence.  Customers should use the latest available IoC logic, update affected NetScaler appliances, preserve evidence when compromise is suspected, and engage their incident response teams for forensic review. The IoC feature is designed to help customers move faster during a security event, but it should be used as part of a broader response process that includes patching, investigation, monitoring, and, when needed, clean redeployment.  Last Updated: October 16, 2026

items.title: Citrix NetScaler ADC and Citrix NetScaler Gateway Security Bulletin for CVE-2026-88771 through CVE-2026-88778
items.summary: Guidance for customers on newly addressed vulnerabilities and recommended updates As the cybersecurity landscape continues to evolve, organizations across the industry are seeing changes in the pace, scale, and complexity of vulnerability research, discovery, and analysis. AI-assisted research and automation may contribute to this shift by enabling faster identification and validation of certain classes of security issues. Citrix continues to invest in secure development, security testing, coordinated disclosure, and vulnerability response processes.   Citrix has released updates for NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway to address multiple security vulnerabilities. These vulnerabilities vary by deployment configuration and enabled features, and include issues that could allow remote code execution, denial of service, HTTP request smuggling, policy bypass, and TCP initial sequence number prediction under specific conditions.  Exploitation of CVE-2026-88771 and CVE-2026-88772 on unmitigated NetScaler deployments has been observed. Citrix strongly urges affected customers to install the relevant updated versions as soon as possible.  Summary of Vulnerabilities CVE ID  Description  Preconditions  CWE  CVSS v4.0  CVE-2026-88771  Remote code execution due to improper input validation that can allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute arbitrary commands.  All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments, including default configuration. No additional features are required.  CWE-20: Improper Input Validation  9.5  CVE-2026-88772  Memory overflow vulnerability leading to remote code execution or denial of service.  DTLS configuration enabled on NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway. DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers.  CWE-119: Improper Restriction of Operations within the Bounds of a Memory Buffer  9.5  CVE-2026-88773  HTTP request smuggling.  HTTP configuration enabled on NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway.  CWE-444: Inconsistent Interpretation of HTTP Requests  9.3  CVE-2026-88774  Feature policy bypass due to improper HTTP URL-based expression usage.  HTTP configuration enabled on NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway.  CWE-16: Configuration  7.0  CVE-2026-88775  Memory overflow vulnerability leading to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or denial of service.  NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway configured as Gateway or AAA virtual server.  CWE-119  8.8  CVE-2026-88776  Memory overflow vulnerability leading to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or denial of service.  Configured as a load balancing virtual server of type Oracle.  CWE-119  8.8  CVE-2026-88777  Memory overflow vulnerability leading to unpredictable or erroneous behavior or denial of service.  Configured as an LB/CS or CGNAT-LSN/NAT64 device with a non-HTTP L7 protocol feature enabled.  CWE-119  8.8  CVE-2026-88778  TCP Initial Sequence Number prediction.  TCP configuration enabled on NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway.  CWE-342: Predictable Exact Value from Previous Values  8.8  What Customers Should Do Customers using affected versions of the NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway products should install one of the following updated versions, or a later release in the same branch, as soon as possible:  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 14.1-73.37 and later releases  NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway 13.1-64.23 and later releases of 13.1  NetScaler ADC 14.1-FIPS 14.1-73.37 FIPS and later releases of 14.1-FIPS  NetScaler ADC 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP 13.1.37.279 and later releases of 13.1-FIPS and 13.1-NDcPP  Customers should review the CVE preconditions below to determine whether their NetScaler deployments are exposed based on enabled services, virtual server types, or system parameters. Where a precondition is met, customers should prioritize updating those NetScaler deployments and continue to monitor official NetScaler security guidance for the latest information. Please note that all NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway are impacted by one or more of the vulnerabilities. Citrix recommends upgrading the versions containing the fix immediately.  Please note this bulletin only applies to customer-managed NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway. Citrix upgrades the Citrix-managed cloud services, including Gateway Service and Citrix-managed Adaptive Authentication, with the necessary software updates.  Steps to Determine Whether a NetScaler Deployment Meets the CVE Preconditions CVE-2026-88771 All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments are affected, including NetScaler deployments with the default configuration. No additional features or settings need to be enabled for the NetScaler deployment to meet this precondition.  CVE-2026-88772 NetScaler deployments meet the precondition only when DTLS is enabled on NetScaler ADC or NetScaler Gateway. Customers should note that DTLS is enabled by default on VPN virtual servers. Relevant configuration patterns to check are as follows:  add vpn vserver vpn1 SSL 10.0.0.0 443 -Listenpolicy NONE  This indicates DTLS is not explicitly disabled, so DTLS is enabled by default.  add vpn vserver vpn1 SSL 10.0.0.0 443 -dtls OFF -Listenpolicy NONE  This indicates DTLS is explicitly disabled, so the precondition is not met.  add vpn vserver vs1 DTLS 10.11.1.1 443  This indicates DTLS is enabled.  add lb vserver vd_dtls DTLS 10.146.111.74 443 -persistenceType NONE -cltTimeout 120  This indicates DTLS is enabled.  CVE-2026-88773  All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments are affected if they use LB, CS, VPN, or Authentication virtual servers of type HTTP or SSL. This vulnerability has been discovered internally. Customers can look for the following configuration patterns to see if their NetScaler deployment meets this pre-condition to check global HTTP parameters and configurations.  add lb vserver <vserver-name> <HTTP or SSL> …  add cs vserver <vserver-name> <HTTP or SSL> …  add vpn vserver <vserver-name> <HTTP or SSL> …  add authentication vserver <vserver-name> <HTTP or SSL> …  CVE-2026-88774 All NetScaler ADC and NetScaler Gateway deployments are affected if they use LB, CS, VPN, or Authentication virtual servers of type HTTP or SSL. This issue has already been addressed in all builds since 14.1-72.X and was reported externally. The vulnerability is related to URL normalization; a URL if not normalized can bypass WAF’s and security rules. For more information on how to normalize a URL in NetScaler, please refer to the public documentation. CVE-2026-88775 Customers can determine whether the NetScaler deployment meets the precondition by inspecting their NetScaler configuration for either of the following strings:   Gateway (SSL VPN, ICA Proxy, CVPN, RDP Proxy):  add vpn vserver .*  AAA virtual server:  add authentication vserver .*  CVE-2026-88776 Customers can determine whether the appliance NetScaler deployment meets the precondition by inspecting their NetScaler configuration for the following string:   add lb vserver.*ORACLE.*  CVE-2026-88777 NetScaler deployments meet the precondition when configured as LB/CS or CGNAT-LSN/NAT64 devices with a non-HTTP L7 protocol feature enabled. Customers should review their configuration for applicable non-HTTP Layer 7 protocol use. Please use the following commands to see if the pre-conditions are being met.  FTP over LB / CS:  enable ns feature LB  add service .* FTP 21  add lb vserver .* FTP .* 21  add cs vserver .* FTP .* 21    FTP over LSN / NAT64:  enable ns feature LSN  set lsn group .* -ftp ENABLED    RTSP over LSN / NAT64:  enable ns feature LSN  set lsn group .* -rtspalg ENABLED    DNS64:  enable ns feature LB  add lb vserver .* DNS .* 53 -dns64 ENABLED  add dns action64 .*  add dns policy64 .*    NAT64:  add nat64 .*  CVE-2026-88778 Customers can determine whether the NetScaler deployment meets the precondition by verifying that both of the following conditions are true:   At least one virtual server is configured with one of the following types: HTTP, SSL, SSL_BRIDGE, TCP, SSL_TCP, FTP, NNTP, RTSP, RDP, DNS_TCP, DOT, SIP_TCP, SIP_SSL, DIAMETER, SSL_DIAMETER, MYSQL, MSSQL, ORACLE, SMPP, MQTT, MQTT_TLS, MONGO, MONGO_TLS, PROXY, SSL_PROXY, USER_TCP, USER_SSL_TCP  AND  The following command returns: Enhanced ISN Generation: DISABLED:  show ns tcpparam | grep "Enhanced ISN Generation"  and confirming that Enhanced ISN Generation is disabled by running: show ns tcpparam | grep "Enhanced ISN Generation".  Additionally, remediating this vulnerability involves modifying the configuration as mentioned in the documentation.  Indicators of Compromise For this release, Citrix is making generic Indicators of Compromise available through NetScaler Console to help customers perform a faster initial assessment of whether NetScaler deployments may have been affected. NetScaler Console’s IoC detection capability is designed to help customers evaluate potential compromises from the Security Advisory workflow. The IoC detection logic may be updated as additional indicators become available, and prior scan results can be retained for later review. Customers who do not use NetScaler Console should contact Citrix Support to request access to the applicable generic IoCs.   This feature is available in both NetScaler Console service and NetScaler Console on-premises with Cloud Connect, starting with version 14.1-73.36. It will appear only after Citrix releases the IoC functionality. Once the detection logic is released, customers can access the feature from the NetScaler Console Security Advisory page, as shown below, where the page will display the date the detection logic was last updated.   Please note that this feature requires the telemetry channel to be enabled. If all prerequisites are met, the feature will be visible to customers who must accept the legal terms and conditions before manually starting the IoC scan.  If customers are unable to use this feature in NetScaler Console, they can contact Citrix Support for assistance executing the IoC scan on their NetScaler deployment.  For more information, please refer to the NetScaler Console documentation.   IMPORTANT NOTE: The IoC Information does not encompass all techniques, tactics, or procedures (“TTPs”) that threat actors might use when targeting relevant environments. Also, threat actors change TTPs and infrastructure frequently. For these reasons and others, the IoC Information might be of limited forensic value and might fail to identify actual compromises. You are advised to retain the services of experienced forensic investigators to assess your environment.  Additional Guidance Citrix continues to monitor vulnerability activity, work with the security research community through coordinated disclosure, and provide timely updates to help customers protect their NetScaler deployments.   Customers should ensure that NetScaler deployments are updated promptly, review configurations against the applicable preconditions, and follow their standard incident response processes if they identify signs of compromise.   To improve security and align with SAML assertion validation best practices, turning off the samlRejectUnsignedAssertion parameter is no longer supported. SAML assertions are always required to be signed and validated. During upgrade, any existing configuration that specifies samlRejectUnsignedAssertion OFF will be automatically converted to the secure default behavior. No administrator action is required. Customers should ensure that their Identity Provider (IdP) is configured to issue signed SAML assertions.  13.1-64.23 has a known issue wherein a NetScaler deployment may go into a cyclic reboot during the upgrade process. This is not a security vulnerability and is only applicable for a specific configuration. Customers can execute the following command to see if their NetScaler deployment is susceptible to this issue.  > show ns variable  If the command returns no output, the NetScaler deployment is not susceptible to this known issue. But if this command shows a list of variables configured in the NetScaler deployment, then please plan to upgrade to 13.1-64.24 to avoid operational issues.  The CVE scan capability of NetScaler Console Security Advisory feature may incorrectly flag NetScaler deployments running 13.1-64.23 as vulnerable. Please note that this is an interim issue and will be rectified as soon as the next Security Advisory update is pushed automatically to your NetScaler deployment. Customers do not need to upgrade NetScaler Console or their NetScaler deployment to address this issue.  Customers can also use NetScaler Console File Integrity Monitoring to help detect unauthorized or unexpected changes to monitored files on managed NetScaler instances. This capability supports ongoing integrity checks and can help customers identify file-level changes that may require further investigation as part of their broader security monitoring and incident response process.  Citrix also strongly recommends that customers forward NetScaler logs to an external logging or SIEM platform to support centralized monitoring, threat detection, forensic investigation, and incident response.  Applying a software update addresses the published vulnerabilities going forward, but it does not remove potential compromise artifacts or prove that exploitation did not occur before the update. If compromise is suspected or confirmed, Citrix recommends deploying a new, updated NetScaler instance rather than relying on the update as a cleanup or remediation mechanism. For more details on that, please refer to the following support article.  The official security bulletin is the authoritative statement concerning the security vulnerabilities announced in the bulletin; please refer to the bulletin as the controlling statement concerning the vulnerabilities.  As clarified during the launch of 15.1 Tech Preview and as stated in the End User Agreement, customers are not permitted to use this firmware in production; the only permitted uses are evaluation and testing. Please note that the NetScaler VPX 15.1 Technology Preview firmware is also vulnerable. A security fix for the 15.1 Technology Preview will be made available shortly.  Learn more and stay up to date Review the official security bulletin  Sign up for security bulletin notifications  Review the NetScaler Secure Deployment Guide  Use NetScaler Console security advisory for your NetScaler deployments.  Last Updated on: September 30, 2026

items.title: NetScaler WAF Signatures Update v183
items.summary: NetScaler has released a new version of its integrated Web App Firewall signatures to help customers mitigate several CVEs with varying CVSS scores.   CVE‑2026‑48282: Adobe ColdFusion is an enterprise application development platform used to build and host web applications, APIs, and business services. Widely deployed in government, enterprise, and public-facing environments, ColdFusion is affected by an arbitrary file upload vulnerability that allows insufficiently validated files to be uploaded to the server. This vulnerability affects supported Adobe ColdFusion installations identified by the vendor advisory and exposes internet-facing application servers to significant risk. Attackers can exploit this flaw by uploading malicious files to vulnerable systems, potentially resulting in remote code execution, complete server compromise, unauthorized access to sensitive data, and persistent control of the affected environment.  CVE‑2026‑32475 :Elementor Pro is a widely used premium WordPress page builder that enables users to create and manage website content through a visual interface. Deployed across a large number of internet-facing WordPress sites, Elementor Pro is affected by an arbitrary file upload vulnerability that permits attacker-controlled files to be uploaded without sufficient validation. This vulnerability affects Elementor Pro versions prior to 4.2.2 and may expose publicly accessible websites to compromise. Attackers can exploit this flaw to upload malicious files that could facilitate webshell deployment, remote code execution, unauthorized access to website resources, and complete compromise of the affected WordPress instance.   Signatures included in v183    Signature rule  CVE ID  Description  998078  CVE-2026-48282  WEB-MISC Adobe ColdFusion - Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability (CVE-2026-48282)  998079  CVE-2026-9586  WEB-MISC Sangoma Switchvox Prior to 8.4.0.2 - Unauthenticated SQL Injection Vulnerability (CVE-2026-9586)  998080  CVE-2026-71362  WEB-MISC Adobe Magento - Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability via createpost (CVE-2026-71362)  998081  CVE-2026-71362  WEB-MISC Adobe Magento - Incorrect Authorization Vulnerability via editpost (CVE-2026-71362)  998082  CVE-2026-32475  WEB-WORDPRESS Elementor Pro Prior to 4.2.2 - Arbitrary File Upload Vulnerability (CVE-2026-32475)  NetScaler customers can quickly import the above signatures to help reduce risk and lower exposure associated with these vulnerabilities. Signatures are compatible with NetScaler (formerly Citrix ADC) software versions 12.1, 13.0, 13.1, and 14.1.  NOTE: Software versions 11.1 and 12.0 are end of life, and you should consider upgrading for continued support. Learn more about the NetScaler software release lifecycle.   If you are already using NetScaler Web App Firewall with the signature auto-update feature enabled, verify that your signature file version is 183 or later and then follow these steps.  Search your signatures for <number>  Select the results with ID   Choose “Enable Rules” and click OK   NetScaler WAF Best Practices  NetScaler recommends that WAF users always download the latest signature version, enable signature auto-update, and subscribe to receive signature alert notifications. NetScaler will continue to monitor this dynamic situation and provide updates as new mitigations become available.  Handling false positives  If app availability is affected by false positives that result from the above mitigation policies, relaxations can be applied. NetScaler recommends the following modifications to the policy.  Modifications to NetScaler Web App Firewall Policy:  add policy patset exception_list  # (Example: bind policy patset exception_list “/exception_url”)   Prepend the existing WAF policy with:  HTTP.REQ.URL.CONTAINS_ANY(“exception_list”).NOT  # (Example:  set appfw policy my_WAF_policy q^HTTP.REQ.URL.CONTAINS_ANY(“exception_list”).NOT && <existing rule>^  NOTE: Any endpoint covered by the exception_list may expose the associated assets to risks   Additional Information  NetScaler Web App Firewall benefits from a single code base across all its form-factors (physical, virtual, bare-metal, and containers). This signature update applies to all form factors and deployment models of NetScaler Web App Firewall.  Learn more about NetScaler Web App Firewall. Read our alert articles and bot signature articles to learn more about NetScaler WAF signatures, and find out how you can receive signature alert notifications.  Please join the NetScaler Community today and engage with your peers to learn more about how they are protecting their businesses with NetScaler WAF.

items.title: What’s New in Citrix SecurSpaces 2026.9
items.summary: Citrix SecurSpaces 2026.9 introduces updates to workspace management, AI usage reporting, shared storage, and developer tools. This release helps teams keep workspaces aligned with project standards, understand AI consumption, and simplify daily development, while giving developers more control over personal settings and workspace recovery. This release includes: Desired state configuration and lifecycle management for workspace templates AI usage reporting by project, user, and model Personal dot files repositories and guided project onboarding AWS Mount Points for shared workspace storage A redesigned extension for VS Code, Cursor, Windsurf, and Kiro Self-service workspace recovery and improved inactivity tracking Updated product naming and more deployment options  Desired state configuration for workspace templatesSecurSpaces now keeps an active link between workspace templates and the workspaces created from them. Each new template-based workspace records its template version, giving project owners a clearer view of which environments use the current standard. Previously, templates supplied the starting configuration. After creation, teams had to coordinate changes to repositories, secrets, extensions, and policies with each developer. Now, project owners can set a default template version and see which workspaces need attention. The Templates page shows counters for workspaces in testing, outdated workspaces, and those with no recorded version. From there, Associated Workspaces groups environments by version and lists their owners. You can also export the list to CSV to plan an update with the team. For example, a project owner can publish a version that adds a shared repository and changes the network policy. Workspace owners then see an update indicator. For workspaces with a recorded published version, the update window previews the configuration changes before they apply them. Applying an update restarts the workspace and replaces its configuration with the default template version. Persistent files, including source code in the home directory, remain in place. However, workspace-specific configuration changes, such as adding a repository or secret, do not carry over. Review the preview before updating. An outdated workspace must also be updated before you can edit its configuration. This helps teams bring the environment back to the current template before making further changes.  Why it matters: Clearer visibility into configuration drift - project owners can identify older template versions and plan updates from a shared view. Controlled workspace updates - developers can review changes and apply the current standard while retaining persistent files.  Guided workspace creation and template lifecycle managementWorkspace creation now opens with a clear choice: use a template, create a custom workspace, or copy an existing workspace. Create from Template carries a recommended label, making the standard route easier to find. Administrators can also enable Require templates for workspace creation on a role. Users with that role create workspaces from templates; the custom and copy options remain visible but disabled, with an explanation. When a template reaches the end of its useful life, you can now archive it. Existing workspaces remain available, while the archived template stops appearing as a choice for new workspaces, including through Quickstart links. You can restore it later if needed. SecurSpaces also prevents deletion of templates and versions that workspaces still use. Together, these controls let project owners introduce, maintain, and retire standard environments. See the workspace template documentation for the full workflow.  Why it matters: Consistent starting environments - role permissions let teams require template-based workspace creation. Controlled template retirement - project owners can archive a template while keeping its existing workspaces available.  AI observability for developer AI usageSecurSpaces 2026.9 adds user, project, and workspace metadata to AI requests it forwards through a configured AI Gateway. This context lets platform teams attribute usage to the people and projects behind it; across the providers their gateway supports. Previously, provider-specific dashboards made it difficult to build a shared view of AI usage across tools and models. Now, teams can report on request volume and token consumption with the workspace context needed to understand who uses those services. The gateway extracts request counts, model names, and token counts, then exports them to your monitoring system. SecurSpaces supplies the workspace context. Report coverage and accuracy therefore depend on the gateway’s support for the providers and request formats in use. The documented reference stack combines Agent Router (formerly Envoy AI Gateway), Prometheus for metric collection and storage, and Grafana for dashboards. A sample Grafana dashboard includes token totals, usage rates, response times, and views by project, user, and model. You can also send gateway metrics to your existing monitoring infrastructure. Administrators can enable gateway health checks and choose how requests behave during an outage. Traffic can bypass an unavailable gateway, leaving a gap in gateway usage reporting, or return an error instead. This makes the choice between continued access and required gateway routing explicit. For setup and reporting details, see Configure AI Gateway routing.  Why it matters: Provider-independent visibility - platform teams can compare AI usage across supported providers by project, user, and model. Better cost attribution - token and request reports provide a basis for cost allocation and chargeback discussions.  Dot files for workspace personalizationDevelopers can now connect a personal dot files repository from Profile > Configuration > Dot Files. SecurSpaces clones it into ~/.dotfiles and runs a supported install script to apply shell, editor, and tool preferences. The configuration uses your connected Git integration and supports private repositories on GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and Azure DevOps. You can apply it to all workspaces you own or select only the ones that need it. For example, your repository might contain shell aliases, editor settings, and a script that installs your preferred command-line tools.
